question: What is the primary reason for proper healthcare waste management?

options.A: To make hospital compounds look neat
options.B: To create more space in the wards
options.C: To reduce the cost of hospital cleaning
options.D: To prevent infection and protect workers

explanation: Proper waste management stops the spread of infections and keeps healthcare staff and patients safe from injuries. [learn more](GNS122_U5_T2#GNS122_U5_T2_h1)

question: What happens when you mix ordinary trash with infectious medical waste?

options.A: The entire batch becomes dangerous infectious waste
options.B: The total volume of waste decreases significantly
options.C: The waste can be safely recycled as normal trash
options.D: The infectious waste automatically becomes harmless

explanation: You've got this! Mixing clean trash with infectious material contaminates everything, which drives up disposal costs and safety risks. Always segregate early! [learn more](GNS122_U5_T2#GNS122_U5_T2_h1)

question: Roughly what percentage of waste generated in a hospital is actually non-hazardous routine rubbish?
explanation: Surprise! The vast majority of what a clinic or hospital produces daily is normal domestic rubbish, just like household refuse. [learn more](GNS122_U5_T2#GNS122_U5_T2_h2)

question: Which of these items should go into the general, non-hazardous waste bin?

options.A: Empty cardboard boxes from IV fluid bottles
options.C: An empty glass vial of chemotherapy drugs
options.D: Gauze soaked with a patient's blood

explanation: Spot on! Clean packaging hasn't touched body fluids or harsh drugs, so it's safe for the general bin. Keep it up! [learn more](GNS122_U5_T2#GNS122_U5_T2_h2)

question: When nurses talk about 'pathological waste', what are they referring to?

options.B: Human tissues, organs, and body parts
options.C: Used food trays and plastic water bottles
options.D: Empty medication boxes and paper files

explanation: Think 'pathology'—it refers to body tissues and anatomical parts removed during surgeries or deliveries. You're doing great! [learn more](GNS122_U5_T2#GNS122_U5_T2_h3)

question: Why must blood-soaked dressings be treated as hazardous infectious waste?

options.A: They contain live germs that can spread disease
options.B: They are made of synthetic plastic fibers
options.C: They take too long to decompose naturally
options.D: They are heavy and expensive to transport

explanation: Items soaked in body fluids carry active pathogens that can easily infect anyone handling them without care. Safety first! [learn more](GNS122_U5_T2#GNS122_U5_T2_h3)

question: Which of these is classified as 'sharps' waste?

options.C: Cotton wool balls and surgical gauze
options.D: Plastic IV fluid bags and tubing

explanation: Easy and clear! Needles and blades have sharp edges that can puncture skin, so they need special handling. [learn more](GNS122_U5_T2#GNS122_U5_T2_h4)

question: What is the biggest danger of carelessly throwing away used sharps?

options.A: Blockage of municipal drainage and sewage pipes
options.B: Transmission of blood infections through accidental pricks
options.C: Creation of unpleasant odors in hospital wards
options.D: Attraction of rodents and insects to the facility

explanation: A stray needle can pierce the skin and directly introduce infections like Hepatitis or HIV into a healthcare worker's bloodstream. Be careful out there! [learn more](GNS122_U5_T2#GNS122_U5_T2_h4)

question: Expired medications and leftover vaccines belong to which waste category?
explanation: You got it! Drugs and medicines always fall under pharmaceutical waste guidelines. [learn more](GNS122_U5_T2#GNS122_U5_T2_h5)

question: Why shouldn't you pour leftover liquid medicines down a regular sink drain?

options.A: It causes immediate blockages in iron plumbing pipes
options.B: It pollutes local water sources and the environment
options.C: It reacts violently with ordinary soap and water
options.D: It produces toxic gases inside the nursing station

explanation: Chemicals flushed down sinks enter our public water systems, harming aquatic life and eventually reaching our drinking water. Protect the environment! [learn more](GNS122_U5_T2#GNS122_U5_T2_h5)

question: Where does radioactive hospital waste usually come from?
explanation: Right on target! Radioactive materials are strictly used in specialized departments like cancer treatment and imaging. [learn more](GNS122_U5_T2#GNS122_U5_T2_h6)

question: What is a major safety risk when dealing with pressurized gas cylinders as waste?

options.A: Gradual chemical corrosion of plastic containers
options.B: Spread of bacterial infections through the air
options.C: Risk of explosion when exposed to high heat

explanation: Pressurized containers can blow up violently if they get tossed into an incinerator or face extreme heat. Safety first! [learn more](GNS122_U5_T2#GNS122_U5_T2_h6)

question: At what point during your shift should you separate (segregate) hospital waste?

options.A: Right at the exact time and place you create it
options.B: After the cleaning staff pack the bins
options.C: When the waste reaches the hospital incinerator

explanation: Always sort your waste immediately as you generate it! Waiting until later leads to mistakes and accidental injuries. [learn more](GNS122_U5_T2#GNS122_U5_T2_h7)

question: You just finished giving an injection. Where should you drop the used syringe and needle?

options.B: An open plastic basin on the trolley

explanation: Brilliant! Sharps always go straight into a rigid, puncture-proof safety box to prevent accidental needle pricks. You're mastering this! [learn more](GNS122_U5_T2#GNS122_U5_T2_h7)
